analysis.one_liner: Requires genetically engineered food to be labeled as such.
analysis.headline: The bill was never voted on: it sat in the Senate Agriculture Committee until the Congress ended, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required any food containing or produced with genetically engineered material to carry a prominent 'GENETICALLY ENGINEERED' label on the package, with restaurants, medical foods, and a few other cases exempted. It would have imposed modest civil fines for unlabeled products, allowed suppliers to give guaranties that shielded downstream sellers from penalties, and excused farmers whose crops were accidentally contaminated by neighboring genetically engineered crops. It also authorized $5 million in research grants into health and environmental risks of genetically engineered food, including allergies and cross-pollination.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who want to know what is in their food — including people with allergies or dietary or religious restrictions who could not otherwise tell whether a product contained genetically engineered ingredients, since more than a third of the soybean crop and a quarter of the corn crop were already genetically engineered at the time. Non-genetically-engineered farmers also gained a liability shield for unintended contamination.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a conspicuous 'GENETICALLY ENGINEERED' notice on any food containing or produced with genetically engineered material, extending the same labeling rights consumers already have for artificial colors, preservatives, and sweeteners.
Cites that over one-third of the US soybean crop and one-quarter of the corn crop were genetically engineered in 1999, meaning most shoppers were already eating these foods without knowing it.

Authorizes $5 million in grants for research into public health and environmental risks of genetically engineered food, including increased allergenicity, toxicity, cross-pollination, and effects on soil ecosystems.
Protects farmers from penalties when their non-engineered crops are unintentionally contaminated with genetically engineered material, as long as they were not negligent.

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers and retailers would bear labeling costs, and seed and agricultural biotechnology companies would face a market risk: some consumers might avoid labeled products. Taxpayers would fund the research grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food makers and biotech seed companies

drawbacks.text: The bill defines 'produced with a genetically engineered material' to include animals fed engineered feed, which would have swept in most meat, dairy, and eggs given how widespread engineered corn and soy feed was — a very broad labeling burden that goes far beyond engineered ingredients themselves.

The warning-style label format ('THIS PRODUCT CONTAINS A GENETICALLY ENGINEERED MATERIAL...') could signal danger where mainstream regulators saw no demonstrated health risk, potentially stigmatizing products without a safety finding, and compliance costs would ultimately flow into food prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is real but informational: shoppers gain knowledge, not a change in what is sold. The main cost falls on food companies, which would need to label or source non-engineered ingredients; critics would call the label format alarmist, while supporters would answer that a right to know does not require proof of harm. The bill's research grants and farmer liability shield show an attempt at a balanced design.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Boxer introduced the Genetically Engineered Food Right-to-Know Act on February 22, 2000.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which was its last action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed.
The bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food and agricultural biotechnology companies were better off, because no labeling requirement was enacted and engineered soy and corn could continue selling unlabeled. Shoppers got no new information about what they were buying.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.role: U.S. Senator from California; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over food labeling
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or report — keeping it from ever reaching the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted a single cosponsor from either party, so no partisan alignment ever took shape in the record.

industries.note: Because the bill died, engineered crops continued to be sold unlabeled, and the industry avoided the market risk that some consumers would buy alternatives if products were marked. The bill's $5 million research program into health and environmental risks also never happened.

The bill would have required them to label or reformulate products containing engineered ingredients, at their expense, and imposed civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation for unlabeled goods. Its defeat spared them those costs.

The bill would have let them market their products as labeled non-engineered and shielded them from penalties for accidental contamination from neighboring engineered crops. With the bill dead, they gained no labeling distinction and contamination liability questions were left unresolved.
